content: Scoliosis in individuals with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) typically progresses over time and is often managed through surgical intervention. However, the current body of evidence does not provide sufficient scientific rigor to definitively recommend spinal surgery for most patients with DMD and scoliosis. This review represents an update, but no new studies were identified for inclusion during the updated search. The primary objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of spinal surgery in patients with DMD who have scoliosis. Specifically, the aim was to determine whether spinal surgery improves survival, respiratory function, quality of life, and overall functional status, as well as to evaluate whether the procedure is associated with significant adverse effects. A comprehensive search was conducted on June 16, 2015, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL Plus. Additional searches were performed in the ProQuest Dissertation and Thesis database (covering January 1980 to June 2015), the National Institutes of Health Clinical Trials Database (as of January 6, 2015), and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (as of June 17, 2015). References from relevant studies were also reviewed. No restrictions were placed on language during the search process. The inclusion criteria for this review required controlled clinical trials with random or quasi-random allocation of treatment, evaluating any form of spinal surgery for scoliosis in patients with DMD. Comparisons could include no treatment, non-operative management, or alternative surgical approaches. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the search results and evaluated study characteristics against the inclusion criteria to determine eligibility for the review. Out of 49 studies identified as potentially relevant, none met the inclusion criteria. All of the studies were either prospective or retrospective case series reviews, rather than randomized controlled clinical trials. In conclusion, due to the absence of randomized controlled trials, there is no high-quality evidence to support or refute the effectiveness of scoliosis surgery in patients with DMD. As a result, no evidence-based recommendations can be made to guide clinical practice. Patients should be informed about the uncertainty regarding the potential benefits and risks of scoliosis surgery. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to evaluate the impact of scoliosis surgery on quality of life, functional outcomes, respiratory function, and life expectancy in this patient population.
